concepts.decision: Choose a test only after naming the recovery claim, systems, participants, safety limits, and acceptance evidence.
concepts.definition: A planned, authorized exercise of the disaster-recovery plan or capability, not a review of its existence.
concepts.failureExample: Calling a document review a DRP test leaves the failover path unproved.
concepts.label: Drp Test

concepts.decision: Write one observable objective before choosing form; reject vague objectives such as “test DR.”
concepts.definition: The precise capability or decision the exercise is intended to prove, such as alternate-site processing or escalation timing.
concepts.failureExample: An undefined objective lets a team declare success although no recovery requirement was measured.
concepts.label: Test Objective

concepts.decision: Include dependencies needed to support the objective and explicitly exclude what must remain protected.
concepts.definition: The bounded people, services, dependencies, locations, injects, and time window included in an exercise.
concepts.failureExample: A test of an application without identity, keys, or network dependencies falsely suggests recoverability.
concepts.label: Test Scope

concepts.decision: Use first when plans are new or changed and the needed evidence is plan logic, not technical recovery.
concepts.definition: A participant-led reading of the plan to check comprehension, contacts, sequencing, and obvious contradictions without operating systems.
concepts.failureExample: A read-through cannot prove that an alternate site, backup, or interface will operate.
concepts.label: Read Through

concepts.decision: Use to expose role, escalation, communication, and policy conflicts with no production action.
concepts.definition: A moderated discussion in which DR-role holders respond verbally to a disruptive scenario and decisions.
concepts.failureExample: Treating a tabletop as a technical failover test hides broken automation or inaccessible backups.
concepts.label: Tabletop

concepts.decision: Use when the plan sequence or a cross-team handoff needs rehearsal before a live capability test.
concepts.definition: A step-by-step rehearsal in which participants trace assigned procedures and handoffs through a scenario.
concepts.failureExample: Skipping a handoff in a walkthrough can leave an unowned restoration decision undiscovered.
concepts.label: Walkthrough

concepts.decision: Use when uncertainty, timed choices, and communications must be stressed safely.
concepts.definition: An exercise using realistic scenario injects to observe decisions, coordination, and response behavior without treating it as an actual outage.
concepts.failureExample: A simulation that announces injects in advance cannot reveal delayed escalation or conflicting authority.
concepts.label: Simulation

concepts.decision: Use when evidence must show alternate operations work but service disruption is unacceptable; authorize resources and data protections.
concepts.definition: A test that operates recovery/alternate capability while normal production remains available.
concepts.failureExample: Running parallel work with unsanitized production data or no reconciliation can create a confidentiality or integrity incident.
concepts.label: Parallel Test

concepts.decision: Authorize only when the assurance need justifies maximum disruption and rollback, communications, and safety controls are ready.
concepts.definition: A scripted exercise that transfers or stops normal operations across the organization to mimic a real contingency.
concepts.failureExample: An ungoverned full interruption can cause real availability loss or confuse incident responders.
concepts.label: Full Interruption

concepts.decision: Set a named stop authority and measurable halt criteria before live actions begin.
concepts.definition: Predefined constraints, stop conditions, escalation path, and rollback limits that keep an exercise from causing unacceptable harm.
concepts.failureExample: If no one can stop an unsafe failover, a test can become the outage it was meant to prepare for.
concepts.label: Exercise Safety Boundary

concepts.decision: Notify the affected roles before and during the exercise, while preserving an unmistakable path for genuine incident escalation.
concepts.definition: Controlled messages that identify the activity as a test, identify channels and approvals, and distinguish exercise signals from a real incident.
concepts.failureExample: An unlabeled alarm during a test can trigger unnecessary external escalation or cause a real alert to be dismissed.
concepts.label: Exercise Communication

misconceptions.claim: A tabletop proves the DR plan will restore systems.
misconceptions.correction: It can expose decision, role, communication, and assumption gaps, but it does not prove technical restoration or capacity.

misconceptions.claim: All stakeholders should receive every exercise detail.
misconceptions.correction: Communicate enough for safe participation and coordination while protecting sensitive recovery, security, and personal information.

outcome: Given a recovery plan and risk boundary, select an exercise form, define objectives and participants, and communicate test status without overstating what the exercise proves.

sections.body: A read-through or tabletop examines plan logic, roles, assumptions, and decisions without changing systems. A walkthrough traces people through a procedure; a simulation introduces realistic injects and observes coordination. A parallel test runs recovery capability while production continues; a full-interruption test takes production service down and therefore demands exceptional authority, safety, communications, and rollback. Select the form from the objective, recovery maturity, service criticality, evidence needed, and acceptable disruption. A test title is not a test objective.
keyPoints: A low-impact exercise can reveal governance and documentation gaps but cannot prove production failover.
The exercise should state entry criteria, stop conditions, success criteria, and evidence owners.
Full interruption is a high-consequence control test, not a default sign of maturity.
sections.title: Choose the exercise for the question

sections.body: Define systems, people, dependencies, data, time window, assumptions, injects, observers, authorized actions, and safety boundaries. Coordinate operations, business owners, suppliers, facilities, security, regulators, customers, and emergency contacts as relevant. Exercise communications should identify test status, expected behavior, channels, approvals, and how a real event will be distinguished from the exercise. Protect sensitive recovery details and preserve logs, decisions, timing, and deviations for later analysis. Stop conditions should be clear enough that any participant can halt an unsafe activity.
keyPoints: Scope controls prevent a test from becoming an uncontrolled outage or security event.
Communication content and recipients depend on exercise form and consequence.
Observers need an evidence plan, not only a meeting invitation.

learningJob.plainExplanation: An exercise proves only what its form, scope, participants, dependencies, and disruption permit it to test. A tabletop can test decisions and coordination, while technical restoration, capacity, and production failover need stronger evidence.
